sentence: In religion Shaivites and goddess worshippers,2 their family deity is Sarasvati, whose chief place of worship is on the river of the same name.
Fair in complexion all are Shaivites in faith, except the Puran readers who, probably in compliment to their Vania and Bhatia patrons, have become followers of Vallabhacharya.
Followers of Vallabhacharya, their family goddesses are Lakshmiji and Chamunda in Marwar.

Shaivites or worshippers of goddesses, they wear the sacred thread, but as they allow widow marriage and eat with Raj puts, Suthars, Luhars, Bharvads, Kumbhars, Ahirs, Rabaris, and Darjis, they are held degraded.
Followers of Ram they belong to the sect of Ramanandis.
Shaivites in religion their family goddess is Bhatarika of Modhera.
Generally well off, they are Shaivites or Yishnavites in religion following the Sam and Yajur Veds.2 The chief place of their family goddess Pratyangira is at Satipur or Sachor in Jodhpur.
Vaishnavs of the Vallabhacharya sect, they follow the Rig, Sam, and Yajur Yeds, and have thirtysix family goddesses, whose temples are in Sorath and Halar in Kathiawar.
Followers of the Yajur Ved, and Shaivites and Vaishnavs in faith, they are a wellto-do class.
Vaishnavs in religion, their family god is Dwarkanath at Dwarka.
Traders and cultivators they are chiefly Shaivites following the Yajur Ved.
Priests of Sompura Salats, they are Shaivs in faith following the Sam and Yajur Yeds.
Shaivs or Vaishnavs in religion their family goddess is Samudri, of Kandolia near Dhoraji in Kathiawar.
They respect Brahmans and belong to the Shaiv, V aishnav, and Svaminarayan sects.
Their family goddess is Hinglaj, and excepting - a few Vaishnavas who belong to the Vallabhdchari sect, they are generally followers of Shiv and Mata.
Especially the Mandalias, Modh V&nias are religious, followers of Vallabhacharya, and careful to visit the shrine of their family goddess Bhadrarika at Modhera.
Though they wear the V aishnav sect-mark, kanthi, they are not strict Vaishnavs.
Shaivs, Vaishnavs, and goddess worshippers, their family goddess is Himja (Parvati) at Raythanpur.
Dining with Vanias and not putting on the sacred thread, they are followers of Vallabhacharya and goddesses.
The Visas are all Thanakvasi 1 or non-image-worshipping Jains ; the Dasas are image-worshipping Jains, Vaashnavs, and Shaivs.
Their women are clever with the needle, flowering silk with much skill and taste.* About the close of the fifteenth century, the Cutch Bhatias were converted to the Vallabhacharya sect of Vaishnavs.

But, unlike the Bhatias, they seldom risk large ventures or push their fortunes in Persia, Arabia, or Africa.8 Yaishnavs of the Ramanuj sect their family goddess is Randel Mata, and they are devout worshippers of the Spirit of the Indus, danja jnr, who is said to have saved them when they fled from Multan.7 Every Lohana village has a place built in honour of this spirit, where a lamp, fed with clarified butter, is kept burning day and night, and where in the month of Chaitra (March- April) a festival is celebrated.
Vaishnavs in name, some of them worship goddesses.
Some among them, of the Vaishnav sect, are strict vegetarians.

The younger women, who are married about sixteen, are generally, by the older women or the family priest, taught to read and write, and learn to sew and embroider.1 Most Jadejas are land-holders, some of them large proprietors, but very many, by want of thrift, and unceasing division of property reduced to be labourers or paupers.2 * 4 In their religion the Jadejas, except a few Yaishnavs, and a still smaller number of Svaminarayans, are half-Hindu half-Musalman.
Some of them are followers of Vishnu, some of Svaminarayan, and some of goddesses.
Though some follow Svaminarayan, most worship goddesses.

In religion chiefly Ramanandis some of them believe in Thakor Mandvi.
Except a few who follow Svaminarayan and Ramanand, they worship goddesses, their favourite family guardians being Amha, Chavan, and Parvati, whose chief place of worship is at Navanagar.
They used to drink liquor and eat flesh, but since they adopted the religion of Svaminarayan they have given them up.
They belong to the Svaminarayan sect.

Devotees and Religious Beggars of various names, Brahmacharis, Sanyasis, Sadhus, Yairagis, Jogis, Khakhis, Atits or Gosais, Kapdis, and Kanphatas, numbered in all 6840 or P85 per cent of the whole Hindu population.

Taking tlicir name from slitting their ears and hanging from the slit a peculiar earring called darshan, they claim as their founder Dhoramnath who, according to Cutch story, among other wonders destroyed Raipur or old Mandvi and dried up the Ran.1 Formerly the Kanphatas were a very powerful body, but as noticed above, about 600 years ago, two of their chief monasteries, at Koteshvar in the west and Ajepal in the east, were wrested from them by mendicants, atits, from Junagad.

The present head, the twenty-seventh in order of succession, was installed in 1879. In former times when any oppression was threatened the Kanphatas, like the Bhats and Charans used to commit trdga, sacrificing one of their number, so that the guilt of his blood might be on their oppressor’s head.1 TheKanphata monastery at Shivramandap2 in Bhuj was established in 1 749 by Rao Desal ji, and given to a Jogi of Dhinodhar.
Like the Dhoramnath Kanphatas they belong to the sect of Shantinath.
They eat with sanydsis, and feed them out of their revenues.3 The third monastery of Kanphatas is that of Kanthadnath at Manphara near Kanthkot in Vagad.
